title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: the paper asks how tall a prismatic column can be before it buckles under its own weight. On this last page Euler checks how badly his earlier load rule, which ignored self-weight (E238 and the 'prima dissertatio'), misjudges such a column.

Setup (from the previous page). A model column has height a and base area dd. It carries the load λ·a·dd, i.e. λ times its own weight, with specific weight set to 1. A second column of the same material has base area bb. The paper found its self-weight critical height as h³ = a³·λ·bb·t/(π²·dd), with t ≈ 200, which gives h ≈ e·a·(λbb/dd)^{1/3}.

The old rule. For similar cross-sections the second moment of area I is proportional to A², so the buckling load is P ∝ A²/L², i.e. P ∝ (base area)²/(height)². Euler writes the load this column could carry, according to that rule, as ξ·hbb, where hbb is its own weight.

The proportion on this page is λ·a·dd : ξ·h·bb = d⁴/a² : b⁴/h². Hence ξ = λa³bb/(h³dd). Substituting h³ gives ξ = π²/t ≈ 9.87/200 ≈ 1/20.

So the rule says this column could still carry one-twentieth of its own weight, whereas in fact it collapses under its own weight alone.

§40. Conversely, whenever the rule says a column can carry only about 1/20 of its own weight, it actually carries nothing. Real columns are always chosen to bear loads far greater than their own weight. Euler therefore concludes that the error from neglecting self-weight is of no practical moment, confirming the claim of the first dissertation.

Modern check. With Greenhill's exact self-weight constant (q·L³/EI = 7.837) the conclusion holds qualitatively, but the numbers do not.
- Cantilever model column (critical load P = π²EI/(4L²)): the self-weight critical weight is k = 4·7.837/π² ≈ 3.18 times the rule's capacity. So t should be about 31, and ξ about 0.31 rather than 0.05.
- Pinned-pinned model column: t ≈ 7.8 and ξ ≈ 1.26.
- Either way Euler's t = 200 is far too large. This reflects the known defect of Euler's self-weight analysis, later corrected by Greenhill (1881) using Bessel functions.
- The engineering conclusion survives, because the self-weight correction is of order W/W_cr, which is small for any practically loaded column (a Dunkerley-type interaction).
errors: The constant t ≈ 200 (hence ξ ≈ 1/20) is quantitatively wrong. With Greenhill's exact critical value 7.837 for a heavy cantilever, ξ = π²/(4·7.837) ≈ 0.31 if the model column is a loaded cantilever; for any standard end conditions ξ is of order 0.3–1.3, not 0.05. This follows from the erroneous critical height carried over from the earlier sections.

The argument in §40 tacitly treats self-weight and end load as separable. It is qualitatively sound (an interaction of the form P/P_cr + W/W_cr ≈ 1), but Euler gives no quantitative estimate of the reduction in capacity for a column that does carry a load.

ideas.what: Scaling rule: buckling load proportional to (base area)²/(height)² for geometrically similar sections
ideas.modern_name: Euler buckling load P = cEI/L² with I ∝ A²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I; 1757/59 E238 'Sur la force des colonnes')
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I; E238; restated in E510

ideas.what: Comparing self-weight buckling with the end-load rule to show that neglecting self-weight is practically harmless
ideas.modern_name: Effect of distributed axial load on buckling; heavy column (Greenhill problem); Dunkerley-type interaction
ideas.where_published: E510 itself; discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (1960)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the concluding remark of a well-known paper on the heavy-column problem. The numerical inaccuracy of Euler's constant is part of the documented history leading to Greenhill's correction. Nothing new appears here.
transcription_corrections: 'ξ b b b' should read 'ξ h b b'
'λa³bb/(b³dd)' should read 'λa³bb/(h³dd)', and 'loco b³' should read 'loco h³'
